clinicalPearls: Defined by the absence of dystopia canthorum, the key clinical feature separating it from type 1.
Congenital sensorineural hearing loss is more frequent and often more severe than in type 1.
Heterochromia iridis and other pigmentary changes are common and may be the most conspicuous feature.
MITF variants underlie the largest subgroup (WS2A); SNAI2 and SOX10 account for further cases.
It is genetically heterogeneous, so a normal MITF result does not exclude the diagnosis.
SOX10-related type 2 can overlap with type 4 and with neurological features, warranting careful phenotyping.
Because facial dysmorphism is subtler than in type 1, diagnosis often rests on the combination of deafness and pigmentary signs.
Autosomal dominant inheritance predominates with variable expressivity; biallelic SNAI2 has been reported rarely.
reference.pathophysiology: Waardenburg syndrome type 2 is a genetically heterogeneous neurocristopathy in which the common thread is deficient development or survival of neural crest-derived melanocytes, but without the periocular changes that cause dystopia canthorum. The largest subgroup results from heterozygous variants in MITF, the master transcriptional regulator of the melanocyte lineage that acts downstream of the developmental pathway involving PAX3 and SOX10; loss of MITF function reduces melanocyte numbers in the skin, hair, iris and cochlear stria vascularis. Additional cases arise from variants in SNAI2 (a transcription factor regulated by MITF) and SOX10 (an early neural-crest transcription factor). Because melanocytes of the stria vascularis are required for endocochlear potential and hair-cell function, their deficiency produces congenital sensorineural hearing loss, which is more penetrant and severe in type 2 than in type 1; the corresponding pigment deficiency gives heterochromia, white forelock and skin depigmentation. The absence of PAX3-dependent periocular mesenchymal effects explains why the inner canthi are normally positioned, defining the type 2 phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 (dystopia canthorum present, PAX3-related)
Waardenburg syndrome type 4 (with Hirschsprung disease, overlapping SOX10 cases)
Tietz syndrome (MITF-related generalised hypopigmentation with deafness)
Non-syndromic congenital sensorineural deafness with incidental heterochromia
Vitiligo and other acquired pigmentary disorders
additionalInvestigations: Audiological testing including newborn screening and pure-tone audiometry
Detailed ophthalmological examination for heterochromia and confirmation of normal canthal position
Canthal and pupillary measurement (W index) to demonstrate absence of dystopia canthorum
Molecular genetic testing of MITF, then SNAI2 and SOX10
Dermatological assessment of pigmentary skin and hair changes
Neurological review where SOX10 involvement or additional features are suspected
Family evaluation and pedigree analysis for autosomal dominant inheritance
redFlags: Severe or profound congenital sensorineural deafness requiring early intervention
Features suggesting SOX10 involvement, such as neurological or bowel symptoms
Signs of Hirschsprung disease indicating possible type 4 overlap
Family history of deafness with pigmentary features identifying at-risk relatives
Failure of language development pending audiological rehabilitation
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and pigmentary features are stable; functional outcome is determined by the sensorineural hearing loss, which is more commonly significant than in type 1 and benefits from early amplification or cochlear implantation. SOX10-related cases may carry additional prognostic considerations.
pitfalls: Excluding Waardenburg syndrome because dystopia canthorum is absent, which actually defines type 2
Stopping the genetic workup after a negative MITF test given the heterogeneity
Overlooking a SOX10 variant that predicts neurological or enteric features
Underestimating the higher likelihood and severity of deafness compared with type 1
Missing subtle pigmentary signs when facial dysmorphism is mild
management: Prioritise early auditory rehabilitation, as hearing loss is more frequent and severe than in type 1, with hearing aids and cochlear implantation for profound loss
Provide early speech, language and educational support for the congenital sensorineural hearing loss
Track hearing from newborn screening through serial pure-tone audiometry
Refer to ophthalmology and dermatology for heterochromia and pigmentary skin and hair changes, with sun protection of depigmented areas
In SOX10-related disease, arrange neurological assessment and surveillance for overlapping type 4 and neurological involvement
Offer genetic counselling recognising genetic heterogeneity, so a normal MITF result does not exclude the diagnosis, with cascade testing of relatives
Coordinate care through an audiology, genetics and ophthalmology multidisciplinary team
